en: Good morning everyone, today I will walk you through our quarterly results.
tamil: அனைவருக்கும் காலை வணக்கம், இன்னைக்கு நம்ம காலாண்டு முடிவுகளை உங்களுக்கு விளக்கப் போறேன்.
context: Opening a team presentation.
explain: 'Walk you through' means explain step by step. 'I will' announces what you are going to do.
usage: Use it to start a presentation to colleagues or a manager.
leelaQ: How do you usually start a presentation at work?
answer: I usually greet everyone and tell them what I will cover.

en: Let me start with a quick overview before we go into the details.
tamil: விவரங்களுக்கு போறதுக்கு முன்னாடி ஒரு சின்ன மேலோட்டத்தோட ஆரம்பிக்கிறேன்.
context: Structuring the start of a talk.
explain: 'Let me' politely says what you will do next. It helps the audience follow your talk.
usage: Use it in a meeting or presentation to introduce the outline.
leelaQ: How do you organise a short talk for your team?
answer: I give a quick overview first and then explain the details.

en: As you can see on this slide, sales have grown by twenty percent.
tamil: இந்த ஸ்லைடுல பார்க்கிற மாதிரி, விற்பனை இருபது சதவீதம் அதிகரிச்சிருக்கு.
context: Pointing to a chart during a presentation.
explain: 'As you can see' draws attention to a visual. 'Have grown' links past growth to now.
usage: Use it when you show a chart or figure to an audience.
leelaQ: What good news did you share at your last meeting?
answer: I shared that our sales have grown this year.

en: That brings me to my next point, which is the budget.
tamil: அது என்னை அடுத்த விஷயத்துக்கு கொண்டு வருது, அது பட்ஜெட்.
context: Moving to the next topic in a talk.
explain: 'That brings me to' is a smooth link between two topics in a presentation.
usage: Use it to move from one topic to the next while presenting.
leelaQ: How do you move from one topic to another when you speak?
answer: I say that brings me to my next point.

en: To sum up, we need more time, more people and a clearer plan.
tamil: சுருக்கமா சொன்னா, நமக்கு அதிக நேரம், அதிக ஆட்கள், தெளிவான திட்டம் வேணும்.
context: Ending a presentation with a summary.
explain: 'To sum up' signals the final summary. Three items in a list sound strong and clear.
usage: Use it at the end of a talk or report to repeat the main message.
leelaQ: How do you end a presentation?
answer: I end by saying to sum up and repeating the main points.

en: Does anyone have any questions before I move on?
tamil: நான் அடுத்ததுக்கு போறதுக்கு முன்னாடி யாருக்காவது கேள்வி இருக்கா?
context: Checking with the audience during a talk.
explain: This question gives the audience a chance to speak. 'Move on' means go to the next part.
usage: Use it in the middle of a presentation or training session.
leelaQ: When do you ask your audience for questions?
answer: I ask after each main part so nobody feels lost.

en: I would like to thank you all for your time and attention.
tamil: உங்க எல்லாரோட நேரத்துக்கும் கவனத்துக்கும் நன்றி சொல்ல விரும்பறேன்.
context: Closing a presentation politely.
explain: 'I would like to' is a polite, formal way to say what you want to do.
usage: Use it as the last line of a formal presentation or speech.
leelaQ: What do you say at the end of a speech?
answer: I thank everyone for their time and attention.

en: Could you please speak a little louder? We cannot hear you at the back.
tamil: கொஞ்சம் சத்தமா பேச முடியுமா? பின்னாடி எங்களுக்கு கேக்கல.
context: Asking a speaker to be louder.
explain: 'Could you please' is very polite. Giving a reason makes the request easier to accept.
usage: Use it in a hall or online meeting when the speaker is hard to hear.
leelaQ: What would you say if you could not hear a speaker?
answer: I would politely ask the speaker to speak a little louder.

en: I'm afraid I haven't finished the slides yet, but I'll share them tomorrow.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், நான் இன்னும் ஸ்லைடுகளை முடிக்கல, ஆனா நாளைக்கு அனுப்பறேன்.
context: Admitting that work is not ready.
explain: 'I'm afraid' softens bad news. 'Haven't finished yet' shows something is still in progress.
usage: Use it with a manager when your work is not ready on time.
leelaQ: What do you say when your work is not ready?
answer: I say I am sorry and promise to send it tomorrow.

en: Let's take a five-minute break and come back at eleven.
tamil: அஞ்சு நிமிஷம் இடைவேளை எடுத்துட்டு பதினொரு மணிக்கு திரும்ப வரலாம்.
context: Suggesting a break in a long session.
explain: 'Let's' makes a suggestion for the whole group. It sounds friendly, not bossy.
usage: Use it when you lead a long meeting or workshop.
leelaQ: When do you take a break in a long meeting?
answer: I suggest a short break after an hour so everyone feels fresh.

en: I truly believe this new system will save us a lot of time.
tamil: இந்த புது சிஸ்டம் நமக்கு நிறைய நேரத்தை மிச்சப்படுத்தும்னு நான் உண்மையா நம்பறேன்.
context: Persuading your team to try a new tool.
explain: 'I truly believe' adds strong feeling. 'Will save' gives a clear promise about the future.
usage: Use it when you try to convince colleagues or a boss about an idea.
leelaQ: What idea would you like to convince your team about?
answer: I want to convince them to use a simpler system.

en: If we start now, we will finish before the festival rush.
tamil: இப்போ ஆரம்பிச்சா, பண்டிகை கூட்டத்துக்கு முன்னாடி முடிச்சிடலாம்.
context: Convincing a partner to start early.
explain: This is a first conditional: if + present, will + verb. It shows a likely result.
usage: Use it to show the benefit of acting early.
leelaQ: Why is it good to start a task early?
answer: If I start early, I will finish without stress.

en: Think about how much money we could save every month.
tamil: மாசா மாசம் எவ்வளவு பணம் மிச்சப்படுத்தலாம்னு யோசிச்சு பாருங்க.
context: Persuading someone with a benefit.
explain: 'Think about' invites the listener to imagine a benefit. 'Could' shows a possibility.
usage: Use it to persuade a family member or a customer.
leelaQ: How do you convince someone to save money?
answer: I ask them to think about how much they could save every month.

en: Why don't we try it for one month and then decide?
tamil: ஒரு மாசம் முயற்சி பண்ணிட்டு அப்புறம் முடிவு பண்ணலாமே?
context: Suggesting a small trial to a hesitant person.
explain: 'Why don't we' is a friendly suggestion. A trial period lowers the other person's fear.
usage: Use it when someone is unsure and you want them to agree to a small step.
leelaQ: What would you say to someone who is unsure about a new idea?
answer: I would ask why we don't try it for one month first.

en: I'm confident that our product will meet your needs.
tamil: எங்க தயாரிப்பு உங்க தேவைகளை பூர்த்தி செய்யும்னு நான் நம்பிக்கையா இருக்கேன்.
context: Talking to a customer about a product.
explain: 'I'm confident that' shows strong belief. It builds trust with a customer.
usage: Use it when selling or recommending something to a client.
leelaQ: How do you build trust with a customer?
answer: I speak honestly and say I am confident about my product.

en: Many of our customers have told us that it makes their work easier.
tamil: எங்க நிறைய வாடிக்கையாளர்கள் இது அவங்க வேலையை எளிதாக்குதுன்னு சொல்லியிருக்காங்க.
context: Using customer feedback to persuade.
explain: Quoting other people is a strong way to persuade. 'Have told' shows past feedback that still matters.
usage: Use it in a sales talk to show that others are already happy.
leelaQ: What do customers say about your favourite shop?
answer: They say the staff are helpful and the prices are fair.

en: Wouldn't it be better to fix this problem now than to pay more later?
tamil: இப்போவே இந்த பிரச்சனையை சரி பண்றது, அப்புறம் அதிகம் செலவு பண்றதை விட நல்லதில்லையா?
context: Arguing for fixing a problem early.
explain: A 'wouldn't it' question makes the listener agree. 'Than' compares two choices.
usage: Use it to convince a manager or family member to act early.
leelaQ: Do you agree that fixing problems early is better?
answer: Yes, I agree because small problems become big if we wait.

en: You may not like the idea at first, but please hear me out.
tamil: முதல்ல இந்த யோசனை உங்களுக்கு பிடிக்காம இருக்கலாம், ஆனா தயவுசெஞ்சு நான் சொல்றதை கேளுங்க.
context: Asking a doubtful listener to be patient.
explain: 'Hear me out' means listen to everything I say before you judge.
usage: Use it when you know someone will resist your idea.
leelaQ: What do you say when you want someone to listen fully?
answer: I say please hear me out before you decide.

en: Our offer is only valid until Friday, so I would suggest deciding soon.
tamil: எங்க சலுகை வெள்ளிக்கிழமை வரைக்கும்தான், அதனால சீக்கிரம் முடிவு பண்ணுங்கன்னு சொல்வேன்.
context: Gently creating urgency with a customer.
explain: 'I would suggest' is a polite way to push. 'Valid until' tells the end date of an offer.
usage: Use it with a client when an offer or price will end soon.
leelaQ: What would you say if an offer is ending soon?
answer: I would tell the customer the offer is valid only until Friday.

en: Let me give you three good reasons why this plan works.
tamil: இந்த திட்டம் ஏன் வேலை செய்யும்னு மூணு நல்ல காரணங்கள் சொல்றேன்.
context: Introducing arguments in a discussion.
explain: Saying the number of reasons first helps listeners follow your argument.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you present your case.
leelaQ: Can you give me one reason to exercise daily?
answer: It keeps me healthy and gives me more energy.

en: Is there any room to lower the price a little?
tamil: விலையை கொஞ்சம் குறைக்க வாய்ப்பு இருக்கா?
context: Negotiating with a supplier.
explain: 'Room' here means possibility. It is a soft way to ask for a discount.
usage: Use it when you bargain with a vendor or supplier.
leelaQ: How do you ask for a better price politely?
answer: I ask if there is any room to lower the price.

en: We can agree to this price if you deliver by the fifth.
tamil: ஐந்தாம் தேதிக்குள்ள டெலிவரி பண்ணா இந்த விலைக்கு ஒத்துக்கலாம்.
context: Making a conditional offer.
explain: 'If' sets a condition. Negotiation often exchanges one benefit for another.
usage: Use it when you agree to a deal only with a condition.
leelaQ: What condition would you put in a deal?
answer: I would agree if they deliver on time.

en: That is a bit higher than we expected, to be honest.
tamil: உண்மையா சொன்னா, இது நாங்க எதிர்பார்த்ததை விட கொஞ்சம் அதிகம்.
context: Reacting to a price that seems high.
explain: 'A bit' and 'to be honest' soften your disagreement but keep the message clear.
usage: Use it when a quotation is more than your budget.
leelaQ: How do you react when a price is too high?
answer: I politely say it is higher than I expected.

en: Let's meet in the middle and settle at fifty thousand.
tamil: நடுவுல சந்திச்சு ஐம்பதாயிரத்துல முடிச்சிக்கலாம்.
context: Suggesting a compromise on price.
explain: 'Meet in the middle' means each side gives a little. 'Settle' means reach a final deal.
usage: Use it when both sides are close but not yet agreed.
leelaQ: When is a compromise a good idea?
answer: It is good when both sides want the deal to happen.

en: We would be happy to continue if the terms are fair for both sides.
tamil: நிபந்தனைகள் இரண்டு பக்கத்துக்கும் நியாயமா இருந்தா தொடர்றதுல எங்களுக்கு சந்தோஷம்.
context: Showing interest but stating a condition.
explain: 'Would be happy to' is polite and formal. 'Terms' means the conditions of a deal.
usage: Use it in business talks to keep the door open.
leelaQ: What makes a deal fair for both people?
answer: Both people should gain something and feel respected.
